title: Linear algebra, conditioning and nonunique solutions
outcome: Solve small linear systems, inspect residuals and distinguish a fitted prediction from an identified coefficient vector.
key_terms: Computing `A \ b` to solve a linear system with a method suited to the matrix, rather than forming an explicit inverse.
Decomposing a square matrix into permuted lower and upper triangular factors once so several right-hand sides solve cheaply.
The number of linearly independent columns, which numerical code estimates with a tolerance on singular values.
The `pinv` result that gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution when a system is rank deficient.
The conjugate transpose written `A'`, which equals the ordinary transpose only for real matrices.
approach: Solve with a factorization, then check the original equation. Worked example A factorizes `[3.0 1.0; 1.0 2.0]` with `lu` and solves for `[9.0, 8.0]`. Worked example B builds a design with two identical `x` columns, so its rank is 2 of 3 and many coefficient vectors give the same fitted values.

exercises.title: Verify a solution
exercises.task: Multiply the computed vector by the original matrix.
exercises.hint: Keep the original equation and units visible.
exercises.answer: A residual is a useful numerical check but must be interpreted alongside conditioning.
exercises.why: `[3 1; 1 2] * [2, 3]` gives 6 + 3 = 9 and 2 + 6 = 8, so the residual `matrix * solution - target` is close to zero.
exercises.wrong: Checking the solution against itself, for example by solving twice, cannot detect a transcription error in the matrix.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `solution ≈ [2.0, 3.0]` and `norm(matrix * solution - target) < 1e-12`.

exercises.title: Reuse a factorization
exercises.task: Double the right-hand side without refactorizing.
exercises.expected: The solution doubles for this linear system.
exercises.answer: Reusable factorization separates setup from repeated solves.
exercises.why: Linearity means `factorization \ (2target)` returns twice the old solution, `[4, 6]`, reusing the same LU factors.
exercises.wrong: Calling `matrix \ (2target)` inside a loop of many right-hand sides refactorizes each time and wastes the setup work.

exercises.title: Expose nonidentification
exercises.expected: Predictions on the design remain unchanged.
exercises.hint: The displacement lies in the null space.
exercises.answer: Fitted-value agreement does not uniquely identify every parameter.
exercises.why: The design has columns `1`, `x` and `x`, so `design * [0, 1, -1]` is zero and adding it leaves every prediction unchanged.
exercises.wrong: Reading the second coefficient as the effect of `x` assumes identification that the duplicated column removes.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `rank(design) == 2` and that `design * alternative ≈ target`.

exercises.title: Interpret a pseudoinverse
exercises.task: Compare coefficient norms in case B.
exercises.expected: The pseudoinverse solution has smaller norm than the shifted alternative.
exercises.hint: Minimum norm is a selection rule among compatible solutions.
exercises.answer: It does not supply missing scientific identification assumptions.
exercises.why: The pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm solution, which splits the slope of 2 evenly to give `[1, 1, 1]` with norm sqrt(3), while the shifted `[1, 2, 0]` has norm sqrt(5).
exercises.wrong: Presenting the pseudoinverse coefficients as the true effects treats a tie-breaking rule as scientific evidence.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `norm(coefficients) < norm(alternative)`; print both vectors and their norms.

exercises.title: Use the correct transpose
exercises.task: Compare adjoint and transpose for the complex vector.
exercises.answer: Matching dimensions alone is insufficient to choose the correct complex inner-product convention.
exercises.why: `values' * values` conjugates, giving |1+i|^2 + |2-i|^2 = 2 + 5 = 7; `transpose(values) * values` does not, giving (1+i)^2 + (2-i)^2 = 3 - 2i.
exercises.wrong: Using `transpose` for a complex norm because the shapes match returns a complex number that is not a length.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `values' * values == 7+0im`, `transpose(values) * values == 3-2im` and `norm(values)^2 ≈ 7`.

exercises.title: Assess sensitivity
exercises.task: Perturb an ill-conditioned problem before trusting its coefficients.
exercises.expected: Inspect conditioning as well as residuals.
exercises.hint: A small residual need not imply stable parameters.
exercises.answer: Numerical accuracy and scientific interpretation require the appropriate assumptions and scales.
exercises.why: A nearly singular matrix can have a tiny residual while its solution swings widely under small changes in the data.
exercises.wrong: Reporting a small residual as proof of reliable coefficients ignores the condition number that multiplies input errors.
exercises.verify: Print `cond(matrix)`, perturb the target slightly and compare the change in the solution with the change in the data; the reference shows `rank([1.0 2.0; 2.0 4.0]) == 1` as a singular case.

checks_note: For complex vectors, `dot` and the adjoint product both conjugate the first argument, giving 7, the squared norm. `transpose(values) * values` skips conjugation and returns `3 - 2im`, so the two operators must not be swapped. `rank([1 2; 2 4]) == 1` detects the dependent rows, and multiplying a two by two matrix by a length-three vector raises `DimensionMismatch`.
